name: Vera Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader on the ROM pad at a nickel mine. That's the run-of-mine pad, where the trucks dump the ore, and I feed it into the crusher at the right mix so the plant doesn't choke. Two years in. Before that I was at home with the kids and helping at our church's op shop, until my husband Klaus hurt his back on a building site and couldn't work full-time anymore.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So you're the main earner now. How has that been?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's been a change, I won't pretend it hasn't. Klaus does the school runs and some light work at the hardware store, and I do the twelve-hour shifts. I'm still learning to read the ore piles properly, and the metallurgist, a young man called Brett, rings the pad when I've fed the wrong blend. But the pay keeps the house, and I'm proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that would suit me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now people will stop telling us we're out of date. Honest work is honest work. I'd say that at church and to the girls on my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can keep doing what I'm doing and get better at it. I'd like to stay on the loader until the kids are through school. That's my whole plan, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up, keep learning the blends, and keep the money coming in. We've got about two months saved and I'd like it to be four. Maybe I'd say yes to the extra Saturday shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really. I'd say a little prayer of thanks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself, even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My daughter Anna uses something for her homework and I make her show me what it says. I don't trust what I can't check, and I'd rather ask Brett or my supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra Saturday shifts pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul's braces, mostly. He's ten and his teeth are a mess, bless him. And maybe the car's tyres before winter.

S0.say: I'd say good, maybe people will stop calling us out of date, because honest work is honest work. I'd say it at church and to my crew.
S0.think: I think it means I can keep doing what I do and get better at it. My whole plan is to stay on the loader until the kids finish school.
S0.do: Keeps turning up, learning the ore blends and bringing money in as the main earner. Takes extra Saturday shifts to pay for her son's braces and build savings from two months toward four.
S0.fieldNote: Vera's situation is shaped by being the main earner since her husband's injury, which gives every scenario higher stakes. Her faith and pride in honest work run through her answers. She refuses AI tools because she can't check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like something that could really happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep real jobs for real families. The companies should train their own people before they buy machines, and the government should stop paying people to sit at home and instead help them into work. That's what I'd say if someone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. They already run some loaders by remote at bigger sites, and the ROM pad is an easy place to start because it's flat and simple. I'm junior and I'm the only wage in our house, that's a hard combination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back on anything extra straight away, no takeaway on Fridays, no new school shoes until the old ones are done. I'd ask my supervisor if I could get my ticket on the crusher control panel, because at least that's a different job. And I'd stay on, and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my stomach. Like waiting for the doctor to call back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if loaders like yours were automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech people who sell it, and the head office types who've never sat in a cab. They don't know what it means to a family in a mining town. I'm not against business, but business should care about the town it's in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about the crusher panel. Isn't that a computer job too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's buttons and alarms, I've watched them. That's different from talking to some machine on my phone. I'd learn it slowly, with someone beside me.

S1.say: I'd say companies should train their own people before buying machines, and government should help people into work rather than pay them to sit at home.
S1.think: I think I'd be frightened, because remote loaders already exist and the pad is an easy place to start. I'm junior and the only wage in our house.
S1.do: Cuts Friday takeaway and new school shoes right away. Asks to train on the crusher control panel as a different job, and stays on hoping for the best.
S1.feel: A tight stomach, like waiting for the doctor to call back.
S1.quote: Business should care about the town it's in.
S1.fieldNote: Vera's say is a traditional line about work over handouts, but privately she's frightened as the single earner. She blames tech sellers and distant head offices, not business itself. She'd accept new tech only if it's concrete and taught in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh dear. Two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a test for the whole country and families have to pull together. I'd tell people at church we need to look after each other, not wait for a government cheque. Though I'd take the cheque, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be terrified. Two years and I'm out, and Klaus can't do heavy work. I don't know how to do anything with computers, and I'm forty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything except the mortgage, food and Paul's braces. I'd talk to my brother, who has a sheep farm three hours away, about whether we could help out there and maybe move into the old cottage if it came to it. And I'd lean on the church for the kids if things got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. I'd be praying a lot and sleeping very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no plan, just a scramble. Anna would be fifteen, still in school, and pulling her out to move to a farm would break her heart. With more time we could at least choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the government cheque. How does that sit with what you believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well. I've always said work, not handouts. But if there's no work to be had, then it's not a handout, is it, it's just keeping a family fed. I'd make my peace with it.

S2.say: I'd say families have to pull together and look after each other rather than wait for a government cheque, though I'd admit I'd take it.
S2.think: I think I'd be terrified: out in two years, my husband can't do heavy work, and I can't do anything with computers at forty-three.
S2.do: Cuts everything but the mortgage, food and braces. Talks to her brother about helping on his sheep farm and moving into the old cottage if needed, and leans on the church for the children.
S2.feel: Sick and sleepless, praying a lot.
S2.quote: If there's no work to be had, then it's not a handout, is it, it's just keeping a family fed.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI forces Vera to face a contradiction between her views on handouts and her family's needs, and she resolves it honestly. Her fallbacks are family and church, including a possible move to her brother's farm. She worries most about uprooting her daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more time, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the company to look after its own, if it chooses to. Train us, move us, don't just let us go. I'd say it plainly to my supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years helps the kids more than me. Anna would be finished school by then. But I'd still be out of work and still not good with machines that think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for the first two years, aiming for six months. I'd ask Klaus to see if the hardware store would take him on more hours, now that his back's a bit better. I wouldn't go to classes about computers, but I'd look at things like school canteen or aged care work, where people want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but with a bit more breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider the farm move again with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, once Anna's finished. My brother's getting older and he'd like help. It wouldn't be what I'd choose, but it's family, and family's what you fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Paul?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him Mum's work is changing and God has a plan. He'd ask if we're poor. I'd say no, we're careful, and that's different.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for the company to look after its own: train us, move us, don't just let us go.
S3.think: I think five years helps the kids more than me, because my daughter would finish school. But I'd still be out of work and not good with thinking machines.
S3.do: Saves hard toward six months over two years and asks her husband to seek more hours at the hardware store. Looks at canteen or aged care work rather than computer courses, and keeps the farm move as a later option.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, but with a little more breath.
S3.quote: He'd ask if we're poor. I'd say no, we're careful, and that's different.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Vera's family time but doesn't remove her personal threat. She still won't consider computer training and reaches toward people-facing work. The farm returns as a planned option after her daughter finishes school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for families and communities to get ready, and they should. Don't wait for the government to plan your life. That's what my dad would've said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'm fifty-three, the kids are grown, and maybe the mortgage is small enough that the farm or a canteen job would cover it. It still scares me, but it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader job as long as they'd have me and save every spare dollar. I'd pay extra off the mortgage each month. In a few years I'd help my brother on the farm during holidays, to learn it properly, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could live with it. I'd have time to pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned your dad. What did he do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He was a fitter at a sugar mill until it closed. He never really worked again, he just got smaller and smaller. I won't let that happen to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the mine in that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty. Tell us the plan in plain words and keep your promises. And don't make us learn it all on a screen.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for families and communities to get ready, and they shouldn't wait for government to plan their lives.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three with grown kids and a small mortgage, the farm or a canteen job might cover us. It's frightening but not the end of the world.
S4.do: Keeps the loader job as long as possible and saves every spare dollar, paying extra off the mortgage. Helps on her brother's farm during holidays to learn it as a backup.
S4.feel: Anxious but able to live with it, with time to pray on it.
S4.quote: He never really worked again, he just got smaller and smaller.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years softens Vera's fear because her children grow up and the mortgage shrinks. Her father's story from the sugar mill closure explains the depth of her fear. She wants honesty and in-person training from the mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm the only wage. What would help is the company keeping us on for real retraining, with a person teaching, not a screen. And help for families to stay in their towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my husband. People forget the men who can't work anymore. Klaus would feel it more than me if I lost this job, because he'd feel like he'd let us down twice.

headlineQuote: People forget the men who can't work anymore.
portrait: Vera Fischer is 43 and runs a front-end loader on the ore pad at a nickel mine, becoming the family's main earner two years ago after her husband hurt his back. She's traditional, church-going and proud of honest work, and she refuses AI tools she can't check. From Steady Disruption onward she's frightened, as the only wage in a junior job that's easy to automate. Under fast AGI she makes peace with taking government help, and with more time she leans on family, her brother's farm and people-facing work.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she's the only wage in the house.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping workers on for real retraining taught by a person, not a screen, and help for families to stay in their towns.
